the concentrations of the target compounds in the indoor air of residences in Los Angeles County were significantly higher than those in outdoor residential air, which were significantly higher than the concentrations measured in the air at a centrally located site.

the concentrations of volatile organic compounds measured in the indoor, outdoor residential (i e, backyard), and centrally located air samples are significantly different, and that there is no relationship between the measured levels of the target compounds at the three locations.
indoor, outdoor, and central air sampling locations are not interchangeable for the assessment of exposure to volatile organic chemicals in residences.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the only way to assess the exposure of an individual to volatile organic compounds is to sample directly at that individual's location.
no single location can be used to predict the other locations, and that each sampling location must be considered independently.
the use of centralized monitoring for assessing personal exposure is not appropriate.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in order to obtain an accurate picture of the exposure of a person to volatile organic compounds, it is essential to collect air samples in the actual location in which the exposure takes place.
, for volatile organic compounds, there are significant spatial variations in concentration, and that a single measurement is unlikely to be representative of a person's exposure.
the best way to assess exposure to air toxics is to measure the actual air that people breathe, either by personal monitoring or by indoor sampling.
